edges.evidence: Dorantes' RomArchive portrait describes him 'reaching into the late romanticist harmony of Falla, Granados, and Albéniz' for compositional and harmonic vocabulary, applying it 'with his Gypsy sensitivity' to flamenco-piano. Albéniz's *Iberia* (1909) is the most direct of the three — the suite already does the work of processing cante-jondo melisma and Andalusian rhythmic cells through a piano-virtuoso harmonic language, the exact gesture Dorantes inverts (flamenco materials rendered through jazz-and-late-Romantic harmony) in *Orobroy*. Held at consensus tier rather than fact because the RomArchive citation is paraphrase rather than verbatim Dorantes quote.

Chano Domínguez's project pages explicitly describe a quartet repertoire that 'explores Falla, Albéniz, Granados, Mompou' rendered through flamenco-jazz piano. The Spanish-nationalist piano repertoire is, for Domínguez, an avowed source — making the Albéniz → flamenco-piano tradition pipeline documentable through Domínguez even where Dorantes' own citation chain is paraphrased.

La leyenda del tiempo (1979) is the founding rupture that made non-traditional instruments — drum kit, electric guitar, sitar, flute — acceptable inside flamenco. Every translation aesthetic in this map descends from that rupture, including Dorantes' 1998 move to put solo piano at the centre of flamenco compás and cante hondo melisma.

Paco de Lucía's Entre Dos Aguas (1973) is the commercial-canonization moment when modernized flamenco became internationally legible — congas, bongos, electric bass entering flamenco for the first time. Dorantes inherits this widened palette and applies it to piano-led flamenco a generation later. Paco's solo-instrument modernization is the precedent Dorantes' generation built on.

Pata Negra's 'blueslería' on Blues de la Frontera (1987) — pure blues at the rhythm of bulerías — is the immediate generational precedent for foreign harmonic vocabulary inhabiting flamenco's body without dissolving it. Dorantes performs the same gesture eleven years later with jazz-piano voicings replacing blues phrasing.

Chano Domínguez (b. Cádiz, 1960) is the methodological elder brother to Dorantes (b. Lebrija, 1969) on the flamenco-piano axis — same materials (post-bop jazz piano + flamenco compás + cante phrasing), slightly earlier in the timeline (Chano debut 1993 vs Orobroy 1998). Domínguez's openly stated dual-influence pairing — Bill Evans + Paco de Lucía — is the public methodological signature both pianists share.

Solo-piano vocabulary — sustained left-hand ostinato over which a singing right hand develops a long-form melisma — is the structural blueprint Spanish music press repeatedly compares Orobroy to. Jarrett's Köln Concert (1975) is the public template for that form. The translation in Orobroy is jazz-piano language imported into flamenco; Jarrett (with Bill Evans) is the source dialect.

Nuevo Día (1975), produced by Ricardo Pachón, is the founding act of nuevo flamenco — explicitly cited as influencing Veneno (1977) and Camarón's Leyenda (1979). Without Lole y Manuel softening cante's pain into something more lyrical, Dorantes' 1998 melisma over a piano ostinato would have less air to breathe in.

El Lebrijano (Juan Peña Fernández) is Dorantes' uncle — same Peña-Perrate-Pinini-Bacán Romani flamenco dynasty of Lebrija and Utrera. Persecución (1976) is the cante-hondo concept-album precedent that the Orobroy lineage descends from on the family side: deep cante carrying long-form poetic narrative material, the methodological precedent for Dorantes' later piano-led re-orchestrations of cante. Family lineage made literal in the separate 2010 duet *Agua, Aire y Fuego* (encoded as its own node on the closure side of the map).

Same family voice across 34 years. Lebrijano's 1976 Persecución cante-hondo concept album and his 2010 duet with his nephew Dorantes on *Agua, Aire y Fuego* bracket Lebrijano's recorded life, with Persecución as the predecessor / artistic statement and Agua-Aire-Fuego as the late-career family-circuit performance. The methodological descent is biological: same cante voice, same Peña-Perrate-Pinini-Bacán dynasty, two generations now sharing the same recording.

The 2010 duet sits on the same album as Orobroy (Nueva versión) — *El tiempo por testigo... A Sevilla* — and is the family-circuit closure pivot of the episode arc. Dorantes returning to Lebrijano's voice on the same record where he re-translates his own 1998 Orobroy: the upward family root and the self-translation event are recorded together. This edge encodes the closure-pivot relationship rather than a temporal influence: the family voice is the audible companion of Dorantes' self-translation.

Paco de Lucía and Camarón's collaboration (Tomatito on the Leyenda sessions) is one of the most-documented partnerships in 20th-century flamenco. Paco's 1973 modernization of flamenco instrumentation was one of the conditions that made the 1979 Leyenda imaginable.

Chano Domínguez has openly cited Bill Evans as one of his two primary influences (alongside Paco de Lucía); Jarrett operates on the same European-jazz-piano axis. Domínguez's solo-piano vocabulary in flamenco is unimaginable without the Evans/Jarrett ECM-era template.

Self-translation edge. The 1998 Orobroy and the 2010 Orobroy (Nueva versión) — both encoded on this single anchor node per nodes-as-singletons rule — are the dual-version frame of the episode. The 1998 version is solo piano with wordless cante melisma; the 2010 version, recorded with a 28-voice children's choir from Seville's Polígono Sur, re-translates the piece into communal song-form. The 12-year gap is treated as a translation event in its own right, the inner mirror of every other edge in this map.

Lágrimas Negras (2003) executes the exact lateral counterpart to Orobroy's translation aesthetic — Cigala's flamenco voice in Bebo Valdés' Cuban piano body, vs Dorantes' jazz-piano language in flamenco's body. Same circuit, same producer ecology (Javier Limón connects Buika and Cigala-Bebo), same five-year window. Both are paradigmatic 'gene wears a different coat' performances.

The 1998 Barcelona International Jazz Festival improvisation that became the Tomatito × Michel Camilo album Spain (2000) is exact-year contemporary with Orobroy (1998). Both pair flamenco virtuoso (guitar / piano) with jazz piano vocabulary — Camilo on the Latin-jazz axis, Dorantes performing both roles inside one body.

Vicente Amigo (b. 1967) and Dorantes (b. 1969) are the same generation of post-Paco solo-instrument flamenco modernizers — Amigo on guitar, Dorantes on piano. Ciudad de las Ideas (2000) and Orobroy (1998) sit two years apart and address the same modernization question from two instruments.

Esperanza Fernández is the deeper-cante female-voice peer occupying the lateral / female-cante slot in this map. Born 1966 in Triana, Seville, daughter of cantaor Curro Fernández and Lebrija-born Pepa Vargas; her debut album *Esperanza Fernández* (2001, BMG) features Dorantes accompanying her on the canonical soleá *En el compás de su sangre* and on the Romani anthem *Gelem, Gelem*. Family-circuit linkage: Dorantes' father and Esperanza's mother are second cousins (deflamenco specialized press). Her voice is on the deep soleá / seguiriya register — the female-cante predecessor to Buika's diaspora-translation work, sharing the Sevillian flamenco geography of Dorantes' Lebrija family. The collaboration is direct and recorded.

Buena Vista (1997) returned aging Cuban son players to international visibility and re-opened the Spanish-Cuban cultural axis Bebo Valdés had been part of pre-exile. Lágrimas Negras (2003) is a direct downstream effect — Fernando Trueba's Calle 54 Records ecosystem and the broader Spanish appetite for flamenco-Cuban dialogue both descend from the Buena Vista breakthrough.

Both Dorantes and Rosalía bring a non-flamenco surface (piano / pop-trap production) into the centre of flamenco compás and cante phrasing while keeping both languages audibly separable. Rosalía's ESMUC flamenco-studies thesis project (2018) is the Gen Z articulation of the same translation aesthetic Orobroy crystallised in 1998.

El Madrileño (2021) extends the post-Rosalía mainstream flamenco-translation pipeline — twelve of fourteen tracks built around collaborations with flamenco / Latin folk / rock figures. The cultural permission for this kind of mainstream album with flamenco at its centre traces backward through Rosalía to the late-1990s flamenco-modernization wave Orobroy belongs to.

edges.evidence: Buika's flamenco-zambra-as-jazz-diva translation on Mi Niña Lola (2006), produced by Javier Limón, sits in the female-cante translation lineage that El Lebrijano's Persecución (1976) opened up — cante hondo on poetic-conceptual material, with foreign instrumentation acceptable. Limón's role connects Buika's project directly to the Cigala-Bebo and broader 2000s-Madrid translation circuit Lebrijano helped seed.

Buika (2006) and Pérez Cruz (2012) sit on the same female song-form translation axis — voice carrying multiple traditions (jazz, soul, fado, flamenco, Cuban, Brazilian) with both languages audibly separable. Pérez Cruz's effortless multilingual eclecticism is the methodological descendant of Buika's earlier diaspora-translation work, advanced one generation.

edges.evidence: Both Rosalía and Llergo studied flamenco at ESMUC in Barcelona under the same teacher, José Miguel Vizcaya 'Chiqui de la Línea'. They are the two most-cited Gen Z female cante voices of the late-2010s — Rosalía leaning urban/electronic, Llergo with deeper inherited cante from her grandfather Pepe in the olive fields of Pozoblanco.

Both released their breakthrough albums into the same 2018-2020 window — El Mal Querer (2018) and Calambre (2020) — and represent the Iberian-Latin American axis of contemporary flamenco-adjacent translation. Peluso (Argentina-born, Spain-based) extends the lineage outside the peninsula.

Carmen Linares is the cante-jondo voice of the same generational cohort as Paco de Lucía and Camarón — the deep-cante root that Dorantes' translation aesthetic flows out of. Lorca's Canciones populares antiguas (1931) — the repertoire Linares records on Flamenco Vivo (1996) — sits in the same poetic recovery line that Lebrijano (Persecución) and Dorantes (Orobroy as wordless cante) participate in.

David Lagos (Jerez) descends from the same dense Sevillian-cante geography that Lebrijano (Lebrija) and Dorantes (Lebrija) occupy. Hodierno (2024) extends Lebrijano's poetic-conceptual cante-with-contemporary-arrangement methodology into the current generation.
